RESULT v1 | k1b7a6537f2 | One immutable event record that fits this need is a Certificate Transparency style log entry as specified in RFC 6962 (the IETF document "Certificate Transparency", published June 2013). The log stores each event as an append-only Merkle Tree Hash leaf: the record contains the raw event bytes (for example, the exact string "TITLE" or "title" plus a locale tag such as tr-TR or en-US), a timestamp, and the log's signature. Entries can never be modified or removed, only appended, because any change would alter the Merkle tree root hash. The verification mechanism is the Merkle audit path defined in RFC 6962 section 2.1.1. An auditor requests the audit path for a leaf index; by hashing the leaf and combining it with sibling hashes, the auditor recomputes the tree root and compares it to the signed tree head the log has published. If the roots match, the record is proven present and unmodified. Inclusion proofs and consistency proofs (RFC 6962 section 2.1.2) let independent auditors confirm the append-only property across tree revisions, so a retroactive edit of a lowercased value cannot be hidden. Why this suits the Turkish dotless i problem: the record stores the original byte sequence, not a normalized form. Any case-insensitive comparison (for example, Turkish "İ".lower() producing "i̇" with a combining dot, or "I".lower() producing "ı" under tr-TR rules) is performed at query time and logged as a separate event referencing the original record. Auditors can therefore re-verify every comparison decision against the untouched original bytes, rather than trusting a lossy pre-lowered field. Because the old token remains valid (RFC 6749 §6 lets the authorization server issue a new refresh token without revoking the previous one), refresh is a pure optimization, not a correctness barrier. That removes the lock from the hot path and reframes the stampede as an *outbound call budget*: at most one refresh in flight per credential key. / Mechanic 1 — request collapsing (single-flight). Key = SHA-256 of (issuer, client_id, subject, scope, refresh-token fingerprint). Keep a mutex-guarded map of in-flight futures. The first caller becomes leader and mints; joiners await the same future; later callers read the cached token. Effect: 10,000 simultaneous misses produce 1 POST to the token endpoint, not 10,000 (this is exactly `golang.org/x/sync/singleflight` semantics). Across processes, swap the map for a Redis lease: `SET refresh:{key} <uuid> NX PX 30000`; only the winner refreshes; release with a compare-and-delete Lua script.
